topics: Long context handling (KV cache, chunking, seq len)
High TPS load patterns and autoscaling/dedicated pools
Fallbacks: model variants and region routing
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 PDT 
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Cho (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Product), Jordan Matthews (Stratus CTO), Lea Kim (SRE), Omar Ruiz (ML Eng), Maya Tan (PM)

[00:00] Alex Cho: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you squeezing this in. quick agenda, we'll demo the edgecases flow — long context, high tps, streaming/backpressure and timeouts and then leave time for Q&A
[00:12] Jordan Matthews: great, excited. our main concern is tail latency and what happens when we hit bursts, like Black Friday style bursts but also we have some long-context chat transcripts 30k tokens plus
[00:25] Samir Rao: yep totally, we'll show both. quick question: what's your peak TPS today and what are you aiming for in the POC?
[00:34] Lea Kim: baseline is about 200 TPS sustained, peaks up to 1.2k for short windows. for the POC we want to validate 3k burst for 5 minutes and ensure errors < 0.1%
[00:46] Omar Ruiz: and long context, some customer support conversations are 25k-40k tokens, we need to preserve KV cache across continuation requests
[00:58] Samir Rao: makes sense. we'll demo 32k context with chunked KV caching and show how the runtime selects quantized kernels. note, the transcription may mis-say some kernel names, but conceptually it's kernel/cuda selection.

[05:10] Demo start - Samir sharing screen (console)
[05:22] Samir Rao: here is the session — first an API call with a 32k prompt. streaming is enabled so you'll see partial tokens sent. we're using Redwood-hosted model, but same config could run on dedicated or private.
[05:37] Samir Rao: starting stream... (stream events displayed)
[05:45] Speaker 1: uh I see tokens coming, a bit choppy in places, is that expected?
[05:50] Samir Rao: yes, with very long context and high token generation rate the runtime may interleave flushes; we do continuous batching and KV cache reuse to avoid re-encoding the entire context each time
[06:10] Samir Rao: if the client has a short read timeout you'll see partial responses and streaming backpressure may cause the runtime to buffer; we expose backpressure signals and you can set low-level timeouts per route in the console
[07:05] Alex Cho: quick note on pricing tradeoffs — long context increases CPU/GPU memory use and may move you to higher instance classes; Optimize will recommend quantization+batch size to reduce unit cost

[10:12] Samir Rao: next, high TPS test. I'm spinning up a synthetic generator to ramp from 200 to 3k TPS over 90s. this is using a dedicated pool with autoscale off so we can see queueing/backpressure
[10:36] (ambient keyboard clacking)
[11:02] Samir Rao: ramping now... requests per second on screen shows 200 -> 800 -> 1500 -> 3k. watch tail latency graph
[11:25] Lea Kim: what's the per-request timeout on the client you're using? our clients default at 5s and we've had timeouts surface in the wild
[11:32] Samir Rao: test client uses 10s read timeout to avoid spurious timeouts; in production you can set 2s/5s depending on expected output length. we also have automatic retries and graceful degradation to smaller models if latency spikes
[12:01] Samir Rao: okay at 3k TPS some requests are being queued; our runtime applies admission control and emits backpressure signals — you'll see the server return 429s with Retry-After when the pool is saturated
[12:28] Jordan Matthews: can you show what happens when a client times out mid-stream? do you have partial output persisted or lost?
[12:36] Samir Rao: good question. by default the server will finish generating and persist logs and KV cache; partial streaming is available to the client if they cancel, but the model run is still accounted for unless you configure early-abort heuristics
[12:50] Maya Tan: and where do those logs live? we have strict data residency and log retention policies
[13:00] Priya Nair: logs can be configured to stay in your VPC via Private deployment or we can ship only aggregated metrics to Redwood. audit logs and request bodies can be disabled or encrypted with your KMS. we cover SOC2/ISO in the security packet we'll send
[13:22] Jordan Matthews: great. are there any cases where streaming actually increases latency because of flushing?
[13:28] Samir Rao: yes, if you have very small-ish increments and frequent flushes you can see overhead; Optimize can recommend chunking size for streaming and batching windows to minimize per-token overhead

[18:40] Samir Rao: switching to failure mode demo — we simulate network flakiness and client timeouts while generating long responses
[18:52] (sound of a network throttle being toggled)
[19:00] Samir Rao: when a network error occurs mid-stream, we show two behaviors: client cancels, server keeps generating and persists to KV cache; OR client reconnects and resumes if you use our resume tokens feature for certain model families
[19:18] Omar Ruiz: resume tokens — is that available across model variants or only same exact model/version?
[19:25] Samir Rao: resume tokens are per model-version and compatible variants we mark as binary compatible. when you switch quantization level or architecture you may lose resume compatibility
[21:05] Alex Cho: question from AE to customer — what's your SLA requirement for p99 latency?
[21:12] Jordan Matthews: p99 of 1.5s for short queries, p99 under 5s for generation up to 1k tokens; for long-context continuity we want < 10% tail errors
[21:28] Alex Cho: ok noted, that's within our Dedicated pool SLA with tuning, we'll include concrete latency targets in the POC plan

[25:40] Samir Rao: let's demo autoscale behavior now — switch to hosted pool with autoscaling enabled, same workload ramp. you'll see additional nodes spin up and queue depth stabilize
[26:02] (graphs updating)
[26:18] Samir Rao: autoscaling has a cool-down and minimum step to avoid flapping; for very short 1-2 minute bursts we recommend reserved capacity with burst lanes instead of relying purely on autoscale
[26:35] Lea Kim: reserved capacity + burst lanes sounds promising, we need cost predictability
[26:43] Priya Nair: yes and Optimize will give you projected unit cost for different commit levels; we can model 6/12 month reserved plans too

[30:10] Jordan Matthews: I'm worried about 429s causing downstream retries and amplifying load — what patterns do you recommend?
[30:18] Samir Rao: backoff + jitter and idempotency for reranks; also set host-side admission control so you fail fast with 429 and client retries use exponential backoff. we also provide sliding window rate-limiter per-route
[30:45] Maya Tan: during the POC can you surface per-token cost and token-level latency so our finance/infra teams can evaluate?
[30:53] Alex Cho: yes, Redwood Console has per-token cost breakdowns and per-route latency. we'll include a sample dashboard and raw logs in the deliverables

[34:00] Demo: streaming backpressure visualization
[34:10] Samir Rao: here is an example where client read timeout of 3s caused the stream to drop; server buffered ~200KB before hitting memory threshold and then applied backpressure and 429s. note that this threshold is tunable per-pool
[34:35] Lea Kim: what's the memory threshold based on? number of inflight streams or total buffered bytes?
[34:41] Samir Rao: it's total buffered bytes per node and per-pool; we also have per-client connection limits to avoid noisy neighbors

[38:20] (brief silence)
[38:30] Jordan Matthews: on security again — if we do Private deployment in our VPC, do you still keep metadata in Redwood control plane? we need an audit trail but not request bodies outside the VPC
[38:43] Priya Nair: correct, in Private you can choose to keep request bodies on the customer side and only surface aggregated metrics to control plane; audit logs can be pushed to your S3/GCS and encrypted with your KMS
[39:05] Jordan Matthews: good. and compliance docs?
[39:09] Priya Nair: we'll send SOC2, penetration test summary, and our network architecture doc as attachments after the call

[42:12] Samir Rao: a couple of implementation tips — for long conversation contexts we recommend prefix windowing + KV caching, and to store embeddings for retrieval-augmented generation instead of re-sending whole chat in every call
[42:32] Omar Ruiz: for our use case retrieval + KV seems right, but how do you handle semantic drift across long sessions?
[42:40] Samir Rao: you can snapshot session state at checkpoints, evict older context using LRU, and Validate output with small eval sets; Redwood Optimize can monitor quality regressions over time

[46:00] Q&A rapid fire
[46:10] Lea Kim: do you support customer-managed keys?
[46:13] Priya Nair: yes, KMS/HSM integrations supported for Private and Dedicated with optional bring-your-own-key
[46:19] Jordan Matthews: how do we route by region?
[46:22] Samir Rao: routing policies per-route, you can prefer region, cost, or latency; automatic fallback to another region is possible with data residency considerations

[50:15] Recap and next steps
[50:20] Alex Cho: recap — we'll send benchmark sheet + raw logs, propose POC plan that covers 3k TPS bursts, long context validation, and streaming timeout/resume testing. action items captured in chat
[50:36] Jordan Matthews: sounds good, can we get pricing ranges for dedicated reserved lanes?
[50:40] Alex Cho: yes we'll include cost model options in the follow-up email

[52:00] End of recording

Notes: transcript has a few transcription artifacts (speaker labels, mis-typed kernel names). Links shared during call: [Benchmark spreadsheet] https://redwood.app/link/benchmarks-ff-789, [Security packet] https://redwood.app/link/security-packet-ff-789, [POC test plan template] https://redwood.app/link/poc-template
